Rosner’s test for multiple outliers

Source: vignettes/outlier-testing.Rmd
outlier-testing.Rmd

This vignette explains Rosner’s generalized extreme Studentized deviate test for multiple potential outliers. It includes the sequential testing procedure, critical values, and the simulation tables used to assess Type I error and determine when warnings are issued.

Related vignettes:

  • Distribution diagnostics, transformations, and probability plots
  • Probability distributions and parameter estimation

rosnerTest

Help topic: rosnerTest.

Let x1,x2,…,xnx_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n denote the nn observations. We assume that n−kn-k of these observations come from the same normal (Gaussian) distribution, and that the kk most “extreme” observations may or may not represent observations from a different distribution. Let x1*,x2*,…,xn−i*x^{*}_1, x^{*}_2, \ldots, x^{*}_{n-i} denote the n−in-i observations left after omiting the ii most extreme observations, where i=0,1,…,k−1i = 0, 1, \ldots, k-1. Let x‾(i)\bar{x}^{(i)} and s(i)s^{(i)} denote the mean and standard deviation, respectively, of the n−in-i observations in the data that remain after removing the ii most extreme observations. Thus, x‾(0)\bar{x}^{(0)} and s(0)s^{(0)} denote the mean and standard deviation for the full sample, and in general

x‾(i)=1n−i∑j=1n−ixj*(1) \bar{x}^{(i)} = \frac{1}{n-i}\sum_{j=1}^{n-i} x^{*}_j \;\;\;\;\;\; (1)

s(i)=1n−i−1∑j=1n−i(xj*−x‾(i))2(2) s^{(i)} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-i-1} \sum_{j=1}^{n-i} (x^{*}_j - \bar{x}^{(i)})^2} \;\;\;\;\;\; (2)

For a specified value of ii, the most extreme observation x(i)x^{(i)} is the one that is the greatest distance from the mean for that data set, i.e.,

x(i)=maxj=1,2,…,n−i|xj*−x‾(i)|(3) x^{(i)} = \max_{j=1,2,\ldots,n-i} |x^{*}_j - \bar{x}^{(i)}| \;\;\;\;\;\; (3)

Thus, an extreme observation may be the smallest or the largest one in that data set.

Rosner’s test is based on the kk statistics R1,R2,…,RkR_1, R_2, \ldots, R_k, which represent the extreme Studentized deviates computed from successively reduced samples of size n,n−1,…,n−k+1n, n-1, \ldots, n-k+1:

Ri+1=|x(i)−x‾(i)|s(i)(4) R_{i+1} = \frac{|x^{(i)} - \bar{x}^{(i)}|}{s^{(i)}} \;\;\;\;\;\; (4)

Critical values for Ri+1R_{i+1} are denoted λi+1\lambda_{i+1} and are computed as:

λi+1=tp,n−i−2(n−i−1)(n−i−2+tp,n−i−22)(n−i)(5) \lambda_{i+1} = \frac{t_{p, n-i-2} (n-i-1)}{\sqrt{(n-i-2 + t^{2}_{p, n-i-2}) (n-i)}} \;\;\;\;\;\; (5)

where tp,νt_{p, \nu} denotes the pp’th quantile of Student’s t-distribution with ν\nu degrees of freedom, and in this case

p=1−α/2n−i(6) p = 1 - \frac{\alpha/2}{n - i} \;\;\;\;\;\; (6)

where α\alpha denotes the Type I error level.

The algorithm for determining the number of outliers is as follows:

  1. Compare RkR_k with λk\lambda_k. If Rk>λkR_k > \lambda_k then conclude the kk most extreme values are outliers.
  2. If Rk≤λkR_k \le \lambda_k then compare Rk−1R_{k-1} with λk−1\lambda_{k-1}. If Rk−1>λk−1R_{k-1} > \lambda_{k-1} then conclude the k−1k-1 most extreme values are outliers.
  3. Continue in this fashion until a certain number of outliers have been identified or Rosner’s test finds no outliers at all.

Based on a study using N=1,000 simulations, Rosner’s (1983) Table 1 shows the estimated true Type I error of declaring at least one outlier when none exists for various sample sizes nn ranging from 10 to 100, and the declared maximum number of outliers kk ranging from 1 to 10. Based on that table, Roser (1983) declared that for an assumed Type I error level of 0.05, as long as n≥25n \ge 25, the estimated α\alpha levels are quite close to 0.05, and that similar results were obtained assuming a Type I error level of 0.01. However, the table below is an expanded version of Rosner’s (1983) Table 1 and shows results based on N=10,000 simulations. You can see that for an assumed Type I error of 0.05, the test maintains the Type I error fairly well for sample sizes as small as n=3n = 3 as long as k=1k = 1, and for n≥15n \ge 15, as long as k≤2k \le 2. Also, for an assumed Type I error of 0.01, the test maintains the Type I error fairly well for sample sizes as small as n=15n = 15 as long as k≤7k \le 7.

Based on these results, when warn=TRUE, a warning is issued for the following cases indicating that the assumed Type I error may not be correct:

  • alpha is greater than 0.01, the sample size is less than 15, and k is greater than 1.
  • alpha is greater than 0.01, the sample size is at least 15 and less than 25, and k is greater than 2.
  • alpha is less than or equal to 0.01, the sample size is less than 15, and k is greater than 1.
  • k is greater than 10, or greater than the floor of half of the sample size (i.e., greater than the greatest integer less than or equal to half of the sample size). A warning is given for this case because simulations have not been done for this case.
